reasons: Passages verified. The TBR unit has the title noun 'Táin' with gen. pl. 'Bó', and 'tána' with 'bó'. The TBC I alarm line (G301012 #50:10) has 'agthar' (agaid, pres. pass. 3pl) with 'baí' (bó, nom. pl.) as subject. Isocrates and Arrian have βοῦς as object of ἀγαγεῖν, of Heracles and Geryon's cattle. RV has gáv- with √aj- in 11 padas (1.33.3b, 2.12.3b, 8.14.8a and others), so the Vedic collocation is real and frequent. Etymology is sound: bó = βοῦς = gáv- (*gʷṓws); agaid and táin (vn. of do-aig, *to-ag-) = ἄγω = aj- (*h₂eǵ-). Both slots are cognate, the relation is the same (verb with cattle as object), and the raid context is comparable in Irish (táin, the alarm cry) and Vedic (Vala, rustling). Against: 'drive cattle' is close to the lexical meaning of *h₂eǵ- itself, so any daughter that keeps both roots will form it. Greek raiding normally uses ἐλαύνω (Il. 1.154), and the Greek anchors are late prose retellings, not formulaic diction. The genre noun táin adds little beyond the verb's basic sense. Plausibly inherited usage, but it cannot be told apart from the generic collocation.

Etymology is broadly sound. Frost: reód and rew < *prews- (Matasović finds the Celtic preform difficult), ON and OE frost, Lat. pruina. Snow: sneachta, snjór, snāw, nix < *sneygʷʰ-. In the Celtic units Irish 'reód' occurs with 'snechta' in 12 of its 30 hits (annals U1111, U1115, LC1115, M1115; M1093 and M1156 have the reverse order). But these are the basic words for two neighbouring winter phenomena, coordinated in weather descriptions, and the order is free: Irish has both orders, Lucretius has nix before pruina, ON has 'sníor' before 'frost'. No frame, epithet or context is shared beyond hard winter. The Irish pivot G600009B is a translation of the Latin Regimen Sanitatis (water of ice or of snow), and OE Azarias paraphrases the Benedicite, so both are derivative. Lucretius's two lines are a philosophical list of weather phenomena. A generic binomial, not phraseology.

Only one element is cognate: cú (pl. 'coin') = canis = κύων. The bird term differs in every language (én, coruus or uulturius, οἰωνός or γύψ), and corp is a Latin loan. Irish passage verified (ZCP 14, Eachtra Conaill Gulban, a late romance, in OCR). Conall demands compensation ('erca') for Corc's foster-father, and Corc answers that nothing will come out of Conall's battalions (OCR 'chathaip', read cathaib) except what dogs carry in their bellies ('ccorpaib'), birds in their claws ('crobaib', OCR 'ccrobazd'), men on their weapons, and what lies under the sod. That is a threat of annihilation in which the slain feed dogs and birds, so the context does match the Homeric dog-and-bird formula and Catullus 108 (vulture, raven, dogs, wolves). But only the dog word is cognate, and the Irish list has four agents rather than the pair. The carrion motif is also widespread in Near Eastern and biblical curses (e.g. 1 Kgs 14:11, Jer 7:33), which a Christian Irish author could take over, and the witness is late. Defensible as continuity, but it rests on one cognate and a widespread motif.

The Irish formula is real and fixed within Irish: a hero takes or gives no foot ('traig', 'troigh') of flight (gen. 'techid', 'teithidh'), with the noun as object of beirid or do-beir. It occurs in the Fer Diad episode (G301026 #9:22 'rugusa'), the Annals of Connacht 1537 ('thuc') and G800012:1:798. Etymology: traig < *treget- < *tregʰ- (Matasović also cites Croat. trag), and techid and (u)teći < *tekʷ- are acceptable. But the Serbian line is no parallel formula. Vuk's recurring line is that no trace of the enemy remains, with the verb 'остане' or 'остаје' and 'трага' rhyming with 'врага'. 'утече' appears only in this single line (Vuk 21700:1053), as a variant of that rhyme formula. Syntax differs: Irish has an object noun with a genitive verbal noun, Serbian a partitive genitive subject. Meaning differs: a foot as a unit of distance against a trace as the smallest remnant. Polarity differs: refusing to flee oneself against the enemy's annihilation. The Serbian no-trace idiom is generic. Coincidence.

The Indo-Iranian side is verified and really formulaic: in the RV, 10 of the 75 padas with hr̥d- also have mánas- (6.28.5d; 7.98.2c, with utá before each noun; 10.177.1b; 10.71.8a), and 10.119.5b has 'hr̥dā́' with 'matím'. Etymology is sound: cride < *ḱr̥d-; menma < *men-men- (formally = mánman-, not = mánas-). The Irish binomial is real (G201011 has 'cride' with 'menman'; G201001 has 'cridhi' with 'mhenmain'). But of its 16 hits in the Celtic units, 15 are religious or homiletic prose (Leabhar Breac homilies, Lives, devotional tracts), and the last is a genealogical gloss. That points to a calque on the Latin heart-and-mind pairing of the Vulgate (Mt 22:37, Dt 6:5) and of liturgy rather than to inheritance. The ON witness (a translated saint's saga: 'hugr', 'hiarta') renews the mind term and is Christian too. Heart and mind is also a near-universal pairing. Genuine within Indo-Iranian; the cross-branch link holds only weakly.

Etymologies hold: loch = Lat. lacus = Gk λάκκος 'pond' (*lok-u-, de Vaan), and OIr. brá or for-brú 'brow' = ὀφρύς (*h₃bʰruH-, Matasović). But it is uncertain that brú 'brink', the word in the frequent Irish phrase on the brink of the lake or sea, is the brow word. The Irish anchor (Ériu 5, Life of Lasair) is an apparatus or variant line in OCR with 'bra'; the regular forms are 'brú' and 'bruach'. The Strabo anchor lacks the claimed collocation: λάκκος is the subject and ὀφρύσι is instrumental (enclosed by high, steep brows), not 'on the brow of the lake'. Greek ἐπί with ὀφρύς and a genitive takes hills, shores and rivers, never λάκκος. Brow for the edge of high ground or a bank is a metaphor any language forms (English brow of the hill), and the prepositions are not cognate. Generic.
checked_loci: Celtic units: 11 hits of for/ar brú with gen. locha/mara

reasons: Exact cognates in a verb-object relation: gonaid = han- and Av. jan- (*gʷʰen-); acc. 'boin' = gā́m (*gʷṓm). The Irish is verified. In the Expulsion of the Déssi (G302006:156-160; LU version G301900 #21:93-96), Dil orders the men not to slay ('gonat') the cow, the horse-boys kill it anyway ('guin'), and he cries woe. Add the Dindshenchas list of forbidden crimes ('guin' with 'blicht') and the stigmatising epithet 'Bóguine'. The idea that killing a particular cow ruins the slayer has a real counterpart in the AV Brahmagavī hymns and in Y 32.14 ('jaidiiāi'). But the Irish case is a one-off magical stratagem (a druid in cow shape), not a general taboo. The Vedic anchor AVŚ 1.16.4 is a protective curse against a demon who kills cow, horse or man. The RV treats killing cattle as ordinary (10.85.13 'hanyante' at the wedding), and only 3 RV padas have gáv- with √han-. Both languages use their default verb and noun. The Dindshenchas list is Christianised. Contexts are only loosely comparable.

Irish verified. G400084:26-27 (Meyer, 'Der Mensch ist Kot', a 14th-century religious poem) is a negated list of pleasant things man is not: nut, brown berry ('dercu'), sloe ('hāirni'), apple ('huball'), then honey, new milk, wine. G109001:328 lists 'cnú', 'áirne', 'uball'. Etymology: uball = ābols (*h₂ébōl) is secure. But áirne (*agrinyo-) ~ Latv. oga (*ōg-) is uncertain: Matasović calls the PIE etymology uncertain and the word formation unclear, with Germanic *akran- the closest match. The nut slot is not cognate (cnú, rieksts). The frames differ: Irish is a negated litany, Latvian a gathering list with pa and the dative ('ogām', 'riekstiem', 'āboliem'), and the sour-apple epithet has no Irish match. Nuts, berries and apples are the obvious wild fruits of temperate Europe, so any forager's list names them. A shared inventory, not a formula.
